**Suggestion:** `max_code_length` is now a required TOML field with no serde default, so any environment still using an older `config.toml` will fail at startup when `Config::new()` parses the file. This is a runtime-breaking config contract change; add a serde default (or make the field optional with fallback) so missing values still resolve to the documented default. [api mismatch]
Severity Level: Critical 🚨 ```mdx - ❌ gRPC server fails to start with older config.toml. - ❌ WebSocket server never starts when config parse panics. - ⚠️ Deployment requires manual config migration for new field. ```
Steps of Reproduction ✅ ```mdx 1. Observe in `src/models/config_models.rs:42-47` that `SessionConfigs` has only non-optional, non-default fields: `session_timeout`, `session_cleanup_interval`, `max_sessions`, and the new `max_code_length: usize`. 2. See in `src/services/helper_services/config_service.rs:19-25` that `Config::new()` reads `CONFIG_FILE` (`config.toml`) and deserializes it with `toml::from_str(&content)` directly into `Config`, which embeds `SessionConfigs`, and then calls `.expect("Failed to parse config file")`. 3. Note that `SessionConfigs` and `Config` have no `#[serde(default)]` attributes and `max_code_length` is not an `Option`, so per serde/toml semantics a `config.toml` missing `session_configs.max_code_length` causes `toml::from_str` to return an `Err` during `Config` deserialization. 4. Run the binary (e.g., `cargo run -- run`) in an environment where the existing `config.toml` predates this PR and omits `session_configs.max_code_length`; `Config::new()` in `src/main.rs:47-52` will invoke `Config::new()`, `toml::from_str` will fail due to the missing field, `expect("Failed to parse config file")` will panic, and the process will terminate before `set_global_config(config)` and server startup. ```

**Suggestion:** This adds a second `get_global_config(...).await` + full config clone inside request validation, even though the same function already acquires global config earlier. Under load, this introduces avoidable mutex contention and extra cloning on every request; fetch the needed value from the existing config read (or cache it once) to avoid hot-path serialization. [performance]
Severity Level: Major ⚠️ ```mdx - ❌ Each ExecuteRequest locks global config mutex twice. - ⚠️ Extra Config clone per request increases CPU usage. - ⚠️ High-throughput workloads see avoidable latency overhead. ```
Steps of Reproduction ✅ ```mdx 1. Start the service via `main()` in `src/main.rs:35-52`, which constructs a `Config` using `Config::new()`, calls `config.init()`, and registers it globally with `set_global_config(config)` from `src/services/helper_services/config_service.rs:66-69`. 2. Send a gRPC `ExecuteRequest` to the `CodeExecutor::execute` method implemented in `src/services/execution_services/executor_service.rs:18-23`; this method immediately calls `ValidationService::validate_request(&request).await` at line 24. 3. Inside `ValidationService::validate_request` (`src/services/validation_services/request_validation/validation_service.rs:61-80`), observe the first call to `get_global_config(|config| config.clone())` at lines 65-67, which locks `GLOBAL_CONFIG` (see `get_global_config` implementation at `config_service.rs:47-57`), clones the entire `Config`, and uses the cloned `session_management_service` to extract the session ID from the request. 4. In the same function, after language and empty-code checks, observe the second call at lines 106-109: `let max_code_length = get_global_config(|config| config.clone()).await.session_configs.max_code_length;`, which again locks the same global `Mutex` and clones the full `Config` just to access `session_configs.max_code_length`, meaning every incoming `ExecuteRequest` performs two global-mutex locks and two full `Config` clones on the validation hot path instead of reusing the earlier config read or caching the needed value. ```
